reference.source: Standard endocrinology reference texts and pituitary tumour consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A rare cause of hyperthyroidism in which a pituitary adenoma inappropriately secretes TSH, driving the thyroid to overproduce hormone
The biochemical hallmark is a raised or inappropriately normal (non-suppressed) TSH in the presence of elevated free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine
This inappropriate TSH pattern must be distinguished from resistance to thyroid hormone, which shows a similar biochemical picture without a pituitary tumour
An elevated alpha-subunit and a raised alpha-subunit to TSH molar ratio support a thyrotropinoma over other causes of inappropriate TSH secretion
Many are macroadenomas at diagnosis and may cause headache, visual field defects and features of other hormone co-secretion (such as growth hormone or prolactin)
Failure of TSH to respond normally to dynamic testing and pituitary MRI showing an adenoma help confirm the diagnosis
Transsphenoidal surgery is the primary treatment, with somatostatin analogue therapy to control hormone secretion and radiotherapy reserved for residual disease
reference.pathophysiology: A thyrotropinoma is a benign monoclonal tumour of pituitary thyrotroph cells that secretes biologically active TSH in an unregulated manner, escaping the normal negative feedback of thyroid hormones. The persistent TSH drive stimulates the thyroid gland to enlarge and to overproduce thyroxine and triiodothyronine, producing central (secondary) hyperthyroidism with a goitre. Because the tumour often retains the capacity to release the glycoprotein hormone alpha-subunit disproportionately, the alpha-subunit to TSH ratio is typically increased. Larger tumours also exert local mass effect and may co-secrete other anterior pituitary hormones.
additionalDifferentials: Resistance to thyroid hormone (thyroid hormone receptor beta mutation)
Assay interference or heterophile antibody artefact
Graves disease and other causes of primary hyperthyroidism
Non-thyroidal illness with abnormal thyroid function
Recent alteration of thyroid hormone replacement
additionalInvestigations: Free thyroxine, free triiodothyronine and TSH demonstrating the inappropriate TSH pattern
Serum glycoprotein hormone alpha-subunit and calculation of the alpha-subunit to TSH molar ratio
Dynamic pituitary testing (e.g. TRH stimulation and thyroid hormone suppression) where available
Pituitary MRI to identify and characterise the adenoma
Genetic testing for thyroid hormone resistance when the biochemistry is ambiguous
Assessment of other anterior pituitary axes for co-secretion or hypopituitarism
redFlags: Visual field loss or other mass effect from a pituitary macroadenoma
Severe thyrotoxicosis with cardiac arrhythmia or thyroid storm
Pituitary apoplexy causing sudden headache and visual or ocular motor deficits
Inadvertent thyroid ablation for misdiagnosed primary hyperthyroidism worsening the pituitary tumour drive
reference.prognosis: With complete surgical removal many patients achieve biochemical cure and resolution of hyperthyroidism, but large or invasive tumours may leave residual disease requiring medical therapy or radiotherapy, and lifelong follow-up is needed to detect recurrence.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting a raised free thyroxine with non-suppressed TSH as an assay error and ignoring it
Treating the thyroid (with ablation or thyroidectomy) instead of addressing the pituitary source
Confusing a thyrotropinoma with resistance to thyroid hormone and missing the tumour
Overlooking co-secretion of growth hormone or prolactin from the same adenoma
references: European Thyroid Association guideline on TSH-secreting pituitary tumours
